newsitem.title: USA: South Korea leaves peace talks hanging in limbo.
newsitem.headline: South Korea leaves peace talks hanging in limbo.

text.p: South Korea's top negotiators in the proposed four-way peace talks said on Monday they were flying back to Seoul after they and U.S. officials failed to persuade North Korea to join the talks.
After a week of hopeful attempts among U.S., North Korean and South Korean officials, a spokesman for South Korea's U.N. mission said of his country's delegation: "They are flying back, all of them."

"They (North Korea) must have realized we cannot regard the so-called acceptance in principle with all those preconditions about four-way talks," Ji Won Suh told said in reference to an increase in food aid that the North demanded.
North Koreans have insisted they could not enter the peace talks between the two Korean nations plus China without guarantees of badly-needed food aid.
Suh said talks would be held on a "working level" which would include South Korean officials from its Washington embassy rather than from Seoul.
In Washington, a State Department official said working group talks had been held in New York on Monday for two hours and "all sides agreed to continue them."
"At this time further work needs to be done and further meetings have yet to be scheduled, but they certainly are possible and the proposal is still on the table," he said.
He refused to comment on the implications of South Korea's departure, saying "they are not able to stay here forever so I am not suprised that they will leave."
Earlier on Monday chief U.S. negotiator Charles Kartman and his South Korean counterpart said they were ready to enter into senior-level talks with North Korea's delegation.

The aim was to hear North Korea's reply to a year-old United States-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War and replace a fraying armistice with a peace treaty.

Although North Korea negotiators told American and South Korean counterparts last week they essentially accepted the proposal, they conditioned that acceptance on demands for more food aid and lifting U.S. trade sanctions,

"At this point ... the North Koreans seem reluctant to come back to the Republic of Korea and the United States for the kind of full working session that we had anticipated," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
He said the peace talks proposal remained on the table but whether Pyongyang will accept it "is anyone's guess. And so there is a bit of a muddle in New York right now."

A high-level North Korean defector, Hwang Jang-yop, who arrived in Seoul on Monday, raised alarms by reporting that North Koreans "have lost hope" and their desperate Stalinist government seems intent on waging war.

Burns said while the border between North and South is one of the most dangerous spots on Earth, the United States, with 37,000 troops there, remains ready to defend South Korea if needed and will maintain its military presence. But he noted that the landmark 1994 U.S.-North Korean accord freezing Pyongyang's nuclear program was working well.

So despite Hwang's comments "we think that actually the events seem to indicate that the North Koreans, at least, are open to further talk with the United States, with South Korea, with Japan, with other countries in Asia who are interested in peace and security on the Korean Peninsula," he said.
On the food aid issue, Burns reiterated earlier comments that if the U.N. World Food Program makes another appeal "We need more. We would obviously look at that very seriously."

The United States already responded twice this year to WFP food appeals for North Korea, contributing $25 million. It has "shown its good faith on this issue (and the already promised aid) may not be the end of the story," Burns said.

"We just hope to assure them that food aid is coming ... through the United Nations and through private voluntary organizations, and that they ought to be assured that we have made a good-faith proposal in the four-party talks," he said.

But North Korea, on the verge of famine, needs far more food than pledged. South Korea and Japan have been holding back to see if peace talks are launched. Also, the North's ability to enter commercial deals is hampered by U.S. trade sanctions.
U.S. officials have said all this is open for discussion once peace talks begin. But Pyongang "wants the issues to be joined," Burns said.
